items.stem: Which of the following statements are true?
statements: There exist three mutually disjoint subsets of ℝ, each of which is countable and dense in ℝ.
For each n ∈ ℕ, there exist n mutually disjoint subsets of ℝ, each of which is countable and dense in ℝ.
There exist countably infinitely many mutually disjoint subsets of ℝ, each of which is countable and dense in ℝ.
There exist uncountably many mutually disjoint subsets of ℝ, each of which is countable and dense in ℝ.
items.explanation: All four are true. Every translate x + ℚ of the rationals is countable and dense, two translates are either equal or disjoint, and there are uncountably many distinct translates since they partition the uncountable set ℝ into countable pieces. Taking three, n, or countably many distinct cosets settles A, B and C.

A.why: ℚ, ℚ + √2 and ℚ + √3 are disjoint (√2, √3 and √3 − √2 are irrational), countable, and dense because each is a translate of ℚ.

B.why: ℚ + k√2 for k = 0, 1, …, n−1 are pairwise disjoint translates of ℚ: the difference of two members would be (k−j)√2, irrational.

C.why: The same family ℚ + k√2 for all k ∈ ℕ gives countably many disjoint countable dense sets.

D.why: The cosets of ℚ in the additive group ℝ, that is the sets x + ℚ, partition ℝ; each is a countable dense translate of ℚ, and there are uncountably many of them because ℝ is uncountable and each coset is countable.

items.stem: Let Z₁ and Z₂ be two independent discrete random variables such that Z₁ follows a binomial distribution with n = 2 and p = 1/2, and Z₂ follows a Poisson distribution with mean 1. Consider the system x₁ − 2x₂ + x₃ = 1, 2x₁ − 5x₂ + 2x₃ = 2, x₁ + 2x₂ + Z₁x₃ = Z₂. Then the probability that the system has infinitely many solutions equals
items.explanation: The coefficient determinant is 1(−5Z₁ − 4) + 2(2Z₁ − 2) + 1(4 + 5) = 1 − Z₁, so the matrix is singular only when Z₁ = 1. Then the second equation minus twice the first gives x₂ = 0 and x₁ + x₃ = 1, and the third equation reads x₁ + x₃ = Z₂: consistent, with infinitely many solutions, exactly when Z₂ = 1. P(Z₁ = 1)P(Z₂ = 1) = (1/2)e⁻¹.
